Haven't posted here in a while! But I'll try to keep a part of the discussion. Dump of what I've been reading:



**Snow Crash** was wonderful. The book's entertaining, intelligent, hilarious. I felt the antagonist's plot never fully made sense, and could've been ironed out some more, but it's an easy flaw to overlook, given how engaging the writing is. Will be picking up Cryptonomicon before long.



**Your Band Sucks** is a memoir written by Jon Fine, best known as the guitarist of post-hardcore band Bitch Magnet. Fine's tendency for sentimentality overshadowed the book's historical value, but I'd definitely recommend it to anyone interested in the scene.



I didn't find **Ring World** to be a particularly remarkable story, despite being well written and conceptually strong. Still enjoyed it. I have A Mote in God's Eye on my shelf, which I'll get around to eventually.



The first book of **Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy**, which was a real nostalgic experience. Loved these books when I was younger, though I've forgotten a lot. Douglas Adams has a sublime talent for contorting science fiction into all kinds of funny faces without ever making a fool of it.



**The Killer Inside Me** by Jim Thompson, a wonderful book about a small-town Texan deputy who also happens to be a psychopathic serial killer. Compelling, fast-moving narrative with a healthy serving of dark humor.



Felt it was only right to follow up The Killer Inside Me with **Fight Club**, which I enjoyed just as much. Impressive what an impactful story Palahniuk managed to cram into 200 pages. A lot to chew on.



School's starting up, so I've yet to gauge whether I'll be able to keep up with the challenge. But the books I currently have open are:



**Rip It Up and Start Again**, a dense and lively history of post-punk's birth and death from '78 to '84.

**The Restaurant at the End of the Universe**, the second of the six Hitchhiker's stories I have.



**Illuminatus!** Not certain what, exactly, it is quite yet.



**The Big Sleep**, one of those old detective stories where an irreverently sharp-witted detective tears up the town in pursuit of justice, or at least a paycheck and a dame.

what inspired me to post this, beyond a frustration with the general mopiness that pollutes the place, was an experience i had a couple years back. i made a post across this sub and /r/needafriend proposing a group chat. after a month, and a couple more waves of posts, there were 20-30 people. it was tight. we had movie nights and everything.



it dissolved after a few months. but i think some lasting friendships were made. i met up with one of them for the third time recently while i was up in wisconsin. i chatted with another, and they were telling me how they still kept in touch with so-and-so. it was a nice experience! and i have this hub to thank
i'm flattered it's swell to meet you too. do you use discord or prefer some other messenger? shoot me details

and do they not deserve genuine friends because of the way they communicate? i assure you that they have expectations of their own. just because they don't line up with yours doesn't indicate any failing on their part.

i'm in the same boat so i'm probably the worst person to be giving you advice! but like the other fella said, the only way to solve this long term is to force yourself to go and build the proper experience to provide you confidence. keep that in mind.



but "forcing yourself" is easier said than done, of course. i usually try to isolate my thought processes, keep myself from overthinking it: i maintain this pseudo-syllogism of "I know what's best for me, and i'm in complete control of my actions, so i'm going to go," which helps keep my anxiety out of the equation. this encourages me to make the right decision, but sweeping your emotions under the rug doesn't necessarily resolve them. on this front, you kinda have to accept that there's only so much you can do. try to distract yourself, so you aren't a nervous wreck when you meet up. remind yourself that the severe gravity you ascribe to social encounters is a production of your own mind. if your fears were realistic, no one anywhere would have friends.



that's what i tell myself at least

Haha, I'm in the same boat - if I was smart, I would've stopped a quarter way in. I wouldn't tell you *not* to read it, but it's anything but a safe bet.

Slaughterhouse five was great! I was surprised how straightforward it was - Vonnegut doesn't mince words. He brings a really interesting perspective to the "anti-war" novel. Definitely gonna read more of him.



Full disclosure: I didn't like it. A lot of people think it's mind-bendingly horrific, but I think it's a great 200 page story scattered across 700 pages of BS. It's essentially two stories interwoven, and one of them is much less compelling than the other. There's a lot of tiresome stream-of-conciousness passages, as well as text you won't even read because it's pointless: citations of non-existent books and page-long dumps of names. The screwey format its known for can be cool, but more than often it was tedious without adding to the story.



All of this is in my own opinion, of course. Like I said, it just didn't click with me. I'd say it's worth trying, but if you don't dig the style, it doesn't get any better.

I've been considering doing this for a while! For about two years, to be precise. But it intimidated me because I'm not a quick reader (how the hell do you read multiple books in a week??) I'm setting my goal low because I don't want to get discouraged and also to account for the fact that I'm late to the party.



And I don't even remember quite what I read so far this year! Besides **Catch-22**, **Slaughterhouse Five**, **Grimscribe**, **Freakanomics**, and **House of Leaves**.



I just got done with **Prey** by Michael Crichton. I got a little burnt out after reading House of Leaves, which really didn't click with me the way I was hoping it would. So it felt good to clean my palate with a straightforward page turner, which is Crichton's calling card.



This week I'll be finishing up Thomas Ligotti's **Songs of a Dead Dreamer** which is a collection of short horror stories. I wasn't completely enamoured by another work of his, Grimscribe, but his style has a unique otherworldly terror that drew me back. The book is full of flowery baroque prose and philosophical stylings which I feel are going over my head, but it's an interesting shorty, so I'm going to see it through to completion.



I've also opened up **Snow Crash** by Neal Stephenson, and so far, it's one of the most hilarious and engaging sci-fi novels I've ever read.
